# Volume 5 — CHAPTER X. THE MANSE GIRLS CLEAN HOUSE

!!! note "Source text"
    Passages cited on the wiki pages link into this page. Only volumes at or before
    this page's cutoff are present.

“Ugh,” Grace said, shivering as she sat up in bed. “It’s raining. A rainy Sunday is something I truly hate. Even if the weather is fine, Sunday is dull enough.”
{: #nw-v05-c10-p0000 }

“Sunday should not be boring for us,” Ida remarked in a slumberous voice, attempting to gather her sleepy thoughts while feeling an uncomfortable certainty that they had slept past the proper time.
{: #nw-v05-c10-p0001 }

“However, it is true that we do,” Grace admitted openly. “Mary Stubbs claims that the majority of Sundays prove so boring she feels like hanging herself.”
{: #nw-v05-c10-p0002 }

“Sunday should be more to our liking than it is to Mary Stubbs,” Ida remarked with regret. “The minister is our father.”
{: #nw-v05-c10-p0003 }

“I desire for us to be the offspring of a blacksmith,” declared Grace with irritation, searching for her stockings. “People would not anticipate superior behavior from us in that case. Simply observe these openings at my heels. They were completely repaired by Mary prior to her departure, yet their condition is just as terrible currently. Rise from bed, Ida. Preparing the morning meal by myself is impossible for me. Oh, my goodness. My desire is for father and Tobias to return home. It would not be expected that father’s absence would be felt so deeply—his presence is scarce even when he resides here. Even so, it feels as though all has disappeared. Checking on Aunt Martha requires me to dash over briefly.”
{: #nw-v05-c10-p0004 }

“Has she improved at all?” Ida inquired upon Grace’s return.
{: #nw-v05-c10-p0005 }

“No, she isn’t,” I was answered. “She continues to groan with the pain. It might be best if Dr. Carrow were informed. However, she refuses—she has never used a doctor in all her days and will not start at this time. Her belief is that doctors merely make a living through the poisoning of folks. Is that what you think they do?”
{: #nw-v05-c10-p0006 }

“No, naturally not,” Ida said, feeling offended. “Dr. Carrow would certainly never poison anyone, I’m positive.”
{: #nw-v05-c10-p0007 }

“Well, once breakfast is over, Aunt Martha’s back will need another rubbing. It would be better if the flannels aren't heated as much as they were yesterday.”
{: #nw-v05-c10-p0008 }

Grace chuckled as she recalled the event. Poor Aunt Martha had almost had the skin boiled off her back by them. A sigh escaped Ida. The exact warmth that flannels ought to have for an aching back would have been known by Mary Stubbs. Everything was known by Mary. Nothing was known by them. And except through harsh experience—for which, on this occasion, the unlucky Aunt Martha had suffered the consequences—how were they to gain knowledge?
{: #nw-v05-c10-p0009 }

The previous Monday, Mr. Ashdown had departed for Nova Scotia accompanied by Tobias to pass his brief holiday. On Wednesday, Aunt Martha was abruptly stricken by a repeated and cryptic sickness that she invariably referred to as “the misery,” a condition that was fairly sure to strike her whenever it was least convenient. Rising from her bed was impossible for her, as every motion produced severe pain. Having a doctor was something she unyieldingly declined. The meals were prepared, and her needs attended to, by Grace and Ida. It is preferable to say as little as possible regarding those meals—though their quality was not significantly inferior to what Aunt Martha had produced. Numerous women residing in the village would have gladly assisted, yet Aunt Martha declined to allow anyone to learn of her predicament.
{: #nw-v05-c10-p0010 }

“Until I can manage to move about, you have to keep struggling,” she moaned. “Blessedly, John is absent. Cold boiled meat and bread exist in abundance, and attempting to prepare porridge is something you can try.”
{: #nw-v05-c10-p0011 }

The girls had attempted it themselves, yet until now they achieved little success. On day one it proved excessively thin. On the following day it was so dense that slicing it was possible. Furthermore, it was scorched on both days.
{: #nw-v05-c10-p0012 }

“I despise porridge,” Grace remarked with venom. “Whenever I possess my own home, I will not permit even one speck of porridge inside.”
{: #nw-v05-c10-p0013 }

“In that case, how will your children manage?” Ida inquired. “Unless children eat porridge, they fail to grow. Everyone agrees on that point.”
{: #nw-v05-c10-p0014 }

“They will need to manage without it or remain small,” Grace countered with obstinacy. “Ida, come and mix this while the table is being set by me. Should I abandon it briefly, the awful mixture is going to scorch. The time is nine thirty. Our arrival at Sunday School is going to be late.”
{: #nw-v05-c10-p0015 }

“Nobody has walked by up to now,” Ida remarked. “It is doubtful that a lot of people will be about. Look at the way it is raining. Also, since there is no sermon, people will not travel from far away to deliver the children.”
{: #nw-v05-c10-p0016 }

“Rupert should be called by you,” Grace said.
{: #nw-v05-c10-p0017 }

As it turned out, Rupert was suffering from a sore throat, brought on by becoming soaked in the Fern Hollow marsh the evening before as he chased dragon-flies. Returning home with soaked boots and stockings, he had remained sitting in them for the rest of the evening. Because he was unable to consume breakfast, Grace forced him to return to bed. Leaving the table untouched, she and Ida departed for Sunday School. Upon their arrival, the school room was completely empty, nor did anyone else show up. Having waited until eleven o'clock, they subsequently returned home.
{: #nw-v05-c10-p0018 }

“It appears there is no one present at the Methodist Sunday School, either,” Ida remarked.
{: #nw-v05-c10-p0019 }

“I’m glad,” Grace said. “I’d hate to think the Methodists had a better record for attending Sunday School on rainy Sundays than the Presbyterians. However, there is no sermon at their Church to-day, either, so it is probable that their Sunday School takes place in the afternoon.”
{: #nw-v05-c10-p0020 }

Ida cleaned the plates, handling them rather well, because Mary Stubbs had taught her that much. Grace gave the floor a rough sweep and prepared the dinner potatoes by peeling them, slicing her finger as she did so.
{: #nw-v05-c10-p0021 }

“If only our evening meal consisted of something other than ditto,” Ida uttered with a sigh. “My weariness of it is complete. What ditto is remains unknown to the Carrow children. Furthermore, pudding is something we are always without. According to Bess, Tabitha’s swooning would occur if Sunday arrived without pudding. Grace, what keeps us from being like everyone else?”
{: #nw-v05-c10-p0022 }

“I have no desire to resemble everyone else,” Grace chuckled while binding her cut finger. “Being me suits me better, as it is far more engaging. Jessie Drew manages a home as capably as her mother does, yet would you wish to share her lack of intelligence?”
{: #nw-v05-c10-p0023 }

“However, our home is not as it should be. That is what Mary Stubbs claims. According to her, folks remark upon how cluttered it is.”
{: #nw-v05-c10-p0024 }

An idea struck Grace.
{: #nw-v05-c10-p0025 }

“We will tidy up everything,” she exclaimed. “Tomorrow we will start immediately. Since Aunt Martha is bedridden and unable to meddle with our plans, this is a truly great opportunity. By the time father returns, we will render it completely beautiful and spotless, exactly as it appeared when Mary left. Sweeping, dusting, and washing windows are tasks anybody can perform. Folks will no longer have reason to gossip about us. Kit Carrow claims that merely old cats gossip, yet the things they say injure us just as deeply as anyone else's words.”
{: #nw-v05-c10-p0026 }

“I hope the weather is good tomorrow,” Ida remarked, full of excitement. “Oh, Grace, being completely washed and resembling everyone else is going to be wonderful.”
{: #nw-v05-c10-p0027 }

“It is my hope that Aunt Martha’s unhappiness continues into tomorrow,” Grace remarked. “If it fails to do so, not a solitary thing will be accomplished by us.”
{: #nw-v05-c10-p0028 }

What Grace amicably desired came to pass. On the following day, Aunt Martha remained too unwell to get out of bed. Rupert likewise continued to be ill and was persuaded without difficulty to remain in bed. How ill the child actually was remained completely unknown to both Grace and Ida; a physician would have been summoned immediately by an attentive mother; however, a mother was absent, and poor little Rupert, possessing a sore throat, a throbbing head, and flushed cheeks, wrapped himself within his tangled bedcoverings and endured his distress in solitude, deriving a degree of solace from a little green lizard kept inside the pocket of his worn nighty.
{: #nw-v05-c10-p0029 }

Summer sunlight saturated the world once the rain had stopped. House-cleaning was ideal on such a matchless day, so Grace and Ida set about their tasks with light hearts.
{: #nw-v05-c10-p0030 }

“The parlour and the dining-room will be cleaned by us,” Grace said. “Meddling with the study would not do, and the upstairs does not matter much. Taking all things out is the first step.”
{: #nw-v05-c10-p0031 }

Consequently, every single thing was removed. The lawn and the veranda held the stacked furniture, and rugs were cheerfully hung over the fence of the Methodist graveyard. A frenzy of sweeping came next, accompanied by Ida’s effort to dust, whereas Grace cleaned the dining-room windows, shattering a single pane and splitting two others during the task. Ida looked uncertainly at the streaky outcome.
{: #nw-v05-c10-p0032 }

“Somehow, they fail to look proper,” she remarked. “Only gleaming and sparkling are the windows belonging to Tabitha and Mrs. Kerr.”
{: #nw-v05-c10-p0033 }

“It doesn't matter. The sunlight passes through them all the same,” Grace remarked bright-heartedly. “With all the soap and water I’ve applied, they have to be sanitary, which is what matters most. Since it has gone past eleven, I am going to clean up this spillage on the floor so we can head outdoors. You can remove dust from the furniture while I beat the rugs. I plan on doing that in the graveyard. Flying dust shouldn't be scattered across the lawn.”
{: #nw-v05-c10-p0034 }

Shaking the rugs brought pleasure to Grace. Flapping and snapping the rugs while standing atop the gravestone of Hezekiah Pollock gave her genuine enjoyment. Naturally, Elder Abraham Clow along with his wife appeared to stare at her with stern displeasure as they drove by in their roomy, two-seated buggy.
{: #nw-v05-c10-p0035 }

“Is that not an awful vision?” Elder Abraham asked with gravity.
{: #nw-v05-c10-p0036 }

“If my own eyes had not witnessed it, I never would have given it credit,” Mrs. Elder Abraham stated with even greater gravity.
{: #nw-v05-c10-p0037 }

Grace enthusiastically brandished a welcome mat toward the Clow group. She was untroubled by the lack of response from the elder and his spouse. It was common knowledge that Elder Abraham had not been seen smiling even once in the fourteen years since his appointment as Sunday School Superintendent. However, the failure of Posy and Adella Clow to return her wave caused her pain. Posy and Adella were dear to Grace. Aside from the Carrows, she considered them her closest schoolmates, and she invariably assisted Adella with arithmetic. Here was a fine example of gratitude. She was snubbed by her companions simply for beating carpets in an ancient cemetery in which, according to Mary Stubbs, nobody alive had been interred for ages. Grace turned abruptly and moved to the veranda, discovering Ida there, deeply upset because the Clow sisters had ignored her greeting as well.
{: #nw-v05-c10-p0038 }

“I guess they are angry about something,” Grace remarked. “Maybe they are envious since we spend so much time playing with the Carrows in Fern Hollow. Well, she can just wait until the school term begins and Adella needs me to demonstrate how her arithmetic should be done! Then we will get even. Come along, let us return the items inside. I am completely exhausted, and I doubt the rooms are going to appear significantly improved compared to before we began—even though I beat out pecks of dust over in the graveyard. House-cleaning is something I despise.”
{: #nw-v05-c10-p0039 }

By the time the exhausted girls completed the two rooms, the hour was two o’clock. After having a dismal bite in the kitchen, they planned to do the dishes right away. Grace, however, chanced to lift a new story-book that Izzy Carrow had loaned her, becoming oblivious to everything around her until the sun went down. Carrying a cup of strong, unpleasant tea up to Rupert, Ida discovered that he was sleeping; consequently, she curled up on Tobias’s bed and likewise drifted off to sleep. In the meantime, a strange tale circulated across Glen St. Agnes, leading people to inquire of one another in all seriousness what ought to be done about those manse youngsters.
{: #nw-v05-c10-p0040 }

“Believe me, that cannot be laughed at anymore,” Miss Winifred said to her husband, sighing deeply. “At the beginning, I was unable to believe it. Ottilie Drew came back from the Methodist Sunday School this afternoon with the tale, and I merely mocked it. However, Mrs. Elder Abraham states that she together with the Elder witnessed it themselves.”
{: #nw-v05-c10-p0041 }

“What did you see?” Ambrose inquired.
{: #nw-v05-c10-p0042 }

“Grace and Ida Ashdown did not go to Sunday School this morning so they could clean the house,” Miss Winifred said, speaking in tones of despair. “Elder Abraham saw them shaking rugs in the Methodist graveyard as he walked home from church, where he had remained to organize the library books. I will never be able to look a Methodist in the face again. Imagine the scandal this will cause!”
{: #nw-v05-c10-p0043 }

An uproar it most certainly caused, becoming increasingly disgraceful as the news traveled, before those over the harbour learned that not merely had the manse children tidied up and hung a laundry load out on the Sabbath, but they had finished off with a graveyard picnic during the afternoon just as the Methodist Sunday School was taking place. The solitary home that stayed happily unaware of the awful event was the manse itself; rain fell once more on the day Grace and Ida lovingly assumed was Tuesday; it poured for the following three days; no one visited the manse; the inhabitants of the manse did not go anywhere; they could have picked their way across the foggy Fern Hollow to Hollowmere, yet every member of the Carrow family, except Tabitha and the doctor, had gone to Brierley on a trip.
{: #nw-v05-c10-p0044 }

“Our bread has run out,” Grace remarked, “and the ditto is finished as well. What are we going to do if Aunt Martha fails to improve shortly?”
{: #nw-v05-c10-p0045 }

“Some bread can be purchased by us in the village, and the codfish that Mary dried is available,” stated Ida. “However, the method for cooking it is unknown to us.”
{: #nw-v05-c10-p0046 }

“Oh, that’s easy,” Grace laughed. “You merely boil it.”
{: #nw-v05-c10-p0047 }

They certainly boiled it; however, because soaking it first failed to cross their minds, its saltiness made it inedible. Although intense hunger afflicted them that evening, the next day brought an end to their hardships. The sun shone on the earth again; Rupert had recovered, and Aunt Martha’s distress departed just as abruptly as its arrival; famine was driven off when the butcher visited the manse. Above everything else, the Carrows came back to their house, and when evening arrived, they, alongside Mary Stubbs and the manse children, gathered again for a sunset meeting in Fern Hollow, in which daisy blossoms floated above the grass similar to dew spirits and fairy-like chimes echoed from the bells on the Tree Lovers within the fragrant twilight.
{: #nw-v05-c10-p0048 }
